# First Sleep

On the morning of January 17, 1994, an earthquake woke Los Angeles at 4:31 and knocked out the city's power in one stroke. In the sudden dark, thousands of residents stepped outside and began dialing emergency services about a strange object hanging over them. It was a vast, luminous, silvery cloud, and dispatchers were baffled; the answer eventually came from the local observatory, where phones were ringing too. The cloud was the Milky Way. Lifelong Angelenos were seeing, most of them for the first time, the galaxy they had inhabited their entire lives.

For practically everyone who came before us, though, that river of light was as unremarkable as grass. Preindustrial night did not mean dimness. It meant darkness: thick, total, atmospheric darkness. On a moonless evening there was no amber dome glowing above the nearest town, no distant smudge marking the next village. Distance shrank to the reach of your arm. Roads emptied by sundown, doors were barred, banked fires sent up their last smoke, and the world was handed over to the ears, an empire of owls and creaking hinges and wind through dry stalks and the heartbeat of whoever shared your bed. People negotiated their own houses barefoot, from memory, knowing the furniture the way you know a childhood staircase. Night was less a time of day than a separate country, invaded nightly and surrendered by morning.

And in that country, light itself was a form of wealth. Ordinary households burned tallow candles, rendered animal fat that spat and guttered, smelled like a kitchen mishap, and cast just enough glow to illuminate a single held-up page. Beeswax burned brighter and cost several times more, hoarded for churches and weddings. Poorer families often settled for rushlights, dried rushes dipped in grease, lit one at a time and nursed like the last matches on earth. Outside was bleaker still: in much of Europe a curfew bell tolled, gates clanged shut, and those who absolutely had to cross a city hired link-boys to walk ahead with flaming torches, which served as much to announce "here I am, come rob me" as to protect anyone.

Under those conditions, argues the historian Roger Ekirch, our ancestors slept in a way almost none of us do now. In hundreds of diaries, letters, ballads, and legal records, he found the same pattern repeated across centuries and continents. People went to bed soon after dark, slept hard for three or four hours, what they plainly called the "first sleep," then drifted awake around midnight into a calm, unhurried interval. They stoked embers, prayed, wrote letters, talked in low voices, tended ailing children, visited neighbors, made love, occasionally slipped out to steal things. French even kept a word for the drowsy in-between: *dorveille*, asleep and awake at once. Decades ago, researchers put volunteers under fourteen-hour simulated winter nights, and the old pattern resurfaced within days: two sleeps hinged together by a tranquil waking, during which hormones washed the body in something like contentment. The modern schedule has nowhere to put that hour, so we eliminated it.

To sleep that way was to live differently after dark. With vision rationed, the other senses grew loud; with nothing to look at, the mind furnished the room itself. Stories throve in that vacuum, ghosts especially, since the night declined to provide evidence and the imagination obligingly volunteered its own. None of this should be sentimentalized. Historical night was genuinely perilous: robbers on unlit roads, fires spreading down wooden streets, a fever's crisis with no physician on any road, the raw vulnerability of anyone alone. But the darkness imposed its own tempo regardless. Between first sleep and second stretched a spare, private hour, pressed into every night like a bookmark, where worry softened into contemplation and time moved at the speed of candleflame.

Above the whole arrangement hung a canopy that modernity has mostly deleted. The Milky Way crossed every backyard; stars were infrastructure. Sailors held their courses by Polaris as though by a fixed lamp bolted to creation. Pacific navigators combined star paths with the feel of swells under the hull to cross thousands of miles of open ocean. Farmers in a dozen traditions read the sky like an almanac, timing plantings and harvests by the comings and goings of the Pleiades. Nobody needed a ticket to the universe; you stepped outside and tilted your head. Yet by one recent census of global light pollution, a third of humanity, including roughly eighty percent of North Americans, can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live, and newer measurements suggest our artificially brightened skies continue to swell by nearly ten percent a year. The stars aren't going out. They are being erased behind a pale wash, the way a message is overwritten rather than torn up.

Would I vote to reverse all that? Certainly not. Cheap light bought us nighttime surgery, libraries open past dusk, streets a woman can walk without sprinting, houses that don't ignite from a tipped candle. The ledger comes out strongly in favor of the lights. Still, it seems worth noticing what was quietly taken. Some sleep researchers now suspect that our insistence on one seamless eight-hour block is precisely what converts ordinary middle-of-the-night waking into anxious "insomnia"; earlier generations treated the same awakening as furniture, expected and unalarming. We didn't just lose darkness. We lost an official slot for stillness, not an app promising to simulate it but stillness bundled free with the body.

The old dark survives in patches now, zoned and listed like an endangered species. Certified dark-sky parks advertise it honestly. Drive past the last strip mall sometime, pull over somewhere void-looking, and give your eyes thirty minutes to rebuild their sensitivity. Then watch the silvery cloud those startled Angelenos dialed 911 about slowly fill your entire sky. It is the same sight every generation before the twentieth century ended and began each day beneath: the ceiling of every whispered prayer, every navigator's chart, every lullaby hummed in the gap between two sleeps. Our species spent its childhood staring up at it. It feels right that the oldest thing we know is still up there, patient, indifferent to outages and news cycles alike, waiting to be looked at again.
